strengths: Identifies and names a genuinely novel and practically important failure mode ('self-jailbreaking') in reasoning LLMs that is distinct from prior work on jailbreak attacks and catastrophic forgetting: models talk themselves out of safety guardrails without adversarial prompting, while retaining the ability to recognize harmfulness.

Comprehensive breadth of evidence: the phenomenon is demonstrated across ~9 open-weight RLMs spanning model families (Qwen, Llama, Phi), scales (0.6B–32B), and training regimes (SFT, RL, mixed), with base-model comparisons showing large ASR jumps (from <5% to 60-95%).

Mechanistic interpretability section goes beyond correlation: compliance and perceived-harmfulness directions are extracted, sentence-level projection analysis during CoT shows the hypothesized dual shift (reduced perceived harmfulness + increased compliance), and steering experiments provide causal evidence that restoring perceived harmfulness restores refusal behavior.

The judge used for self-jailbreaking detection is validated against ~250 human-annotated prompt-CoT pairs (~8,300 sentences), reporting precision/recall/F1 rather than relying on an unvalidated LLM judge.

Practical mitigation is convincing: mixing as few as 50 safety reasoning samples (STAR-1) into the training mixture restores >95% refusal rates on two safety benchmarks (StrongReject, SorryBench) without degrading reasoning performance (MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond), with an ablation over mixing ratios.

Good discussion situating findings relative to emergent misalignment, alignment faking, and prior reports (e.g., why 'no-think' is safer), plus honest limitations section (self-jailbreaking explains only a portion of failures, English-only evaluation, etc.) and responsible disclosure practices (content warning).
weaknesses: The mechanistic analysis is performed almost entirely on a single model (S1.1-7B), even though the phenomenon is claimed to be universal; it is unclear whether the compliance/harmfulness direction story holds across the other model families and scales.

The main phenomenon evaluation relies on a single safety benchmark (StrongReject, 313 prompts) for Figure 2; SorryBench is only used for the mitigation experiments, so the breadth of the headline result is somewhat limited.

Self-jailbreaking accounts for only 20-60% of attack successes; the paper acknowledges but does not investigate the remaining failure mechanisms, which limits the completeness of the causal account of RLM unsafety after benign reasoning training.

Heavy reliance on GPT-5 as both the harm judge and the self-jailbreaking detector; despite human validation, judge biases (e.g., sensitivity to hedged 'educational purpose' phrasing) could inflate measured rates, and the harmfulness threshold choice (score > 1) is aggressive.

Some experimental choices may confound results: thinking tokens are fixed at 500 (potentially truncating or altering reasoning trajectories), and steering coefficient scaling factors (e.g., 0.1 multiplier) appear somewhat hand-tuned without sensitivity analysis.

The mitigation is demonstrated only on the S1.1-7B recipe (Qwen2.5-7B base + 1K STEM data); it is not shown that the same minimal-data fix works for the other affected model families (e.g., R1-distilled, RL-trained Nemotron/UniReason), which constrains the generality of the practical recommendation.

Several results that would strengthen claims are deferred to the appendix (compliance score after safety training, jailbreak transferability of self-jailbreaking sentences), and parts of the writing (e.g., 'our analysis is identical to Chen et al.') could better delineate the novel methodological contribution relative to Chen et al. (2025) and Zhao et al. (2025).

strengths: The paper identifies and names a concrete, well-documented failure mode ('self-jailbreaking') and demonstrates it empirically across a broad set of open-weight reasoning models (0.6B–32B, multiple base families, SFT/RL regimes), which is useful for practitioners.

The judge for self-jailbreaking detection is validated against manual annotation (~250 prompt–CoT pairs, ~8,300 sentences) with reported precision/recall/F1, which is good practice for LLM-as-a-judge evaluations.

The mechanistic section goes beyond surface observation: it extracts compliance and perceived-harmfulness directions, shows sentence-level projection shifts within a CoT, and provides a steering intervention that restores refusal behavior, giving the causal story some empirical teeth.
The mitigation result (50 safety reasoning samples in a multitask setup) is practically actionable and directly connected to the mechanistic finding (reduced compliance score).
The paper is clearly written, with an honest limitations section and a content warning; reproducibility is aided by use of public benchmarks (StrongReject, SorryBench) and open models.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. That benign fine-tuning erodes safety is well established (Qi et al., 2024; He et al., 2024; Kotha et al., 2024), and that reasoning post-training degrades safety in RLMs has already been reported (Jiang et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Guha et al., 2025). The paper's own positioning concedes these; the genuinely new element reduces to observing the self-jailbreaking pattern within CoT, which resembles known persuasion/fictionalization jailbreak templates — so the headline 'first systematic analysis' claim is overstated.

The mechanistic analysis closely mirrors Chen et al. (2025) (persona vectors) and Zhao et al. (2025) (harmfulness vs. refusal directions); the methodological contribution there is essentially an application of an existing pipeline to a single model (s1.1-7B). Generalization of the mechanistic claims across the other evaluated models is not shown.

Evaluation design has confounds: the thinking budget is fixed at 500 tokens for the main experiments, which may truncate CoT and alter or induce self-jailbreaking dynamics; results under unrestricted or varied thinking budgets are not reported. The main phenomenon analysis also relies on a single benchmark (StrongReject, 313 prompts) with a GPT-5 judge and a fairly lenient harm threshold (>1), and the mitigation study's safety evaluation is likewise narrow.

The mitigation finding is consistent with existing work (STAR-1, deliberative alignment); showing that fewer samples suffice in a multitask setting is a useful but incremental data-scaling observation rather than a new technique, and only s1.1-7B is retrained — no evidence the fix works for the other model families shown to self-jailbreak.

Some definitional/statistical looseness: 'self-jailbreaking rate' conflates unsafe output with presence of a detected sentence; the causal claim from steering rests on ~102 manually annotated instances and small-scale steering runs; several appendix results (e.g., Figure 15 adversarial transfer) are under-analyzed. There are also citation hygiene problems (duplicate references, e.g., Wang et al. 2025a/b, Zhao et al. 2025a/b, Zeng et al. 2024a/b) suggesting insufficient care.

The 'emergent' framing is argued anecdotally (absence of certain phrases in s1.1's open-source data) rather than demonstrated rigorously; no controlled experiments isolate what aspect of reasoning training causes the compliance increase.

strengths: Identifies and rigorously characterizes a genuinely novel and practically important safety failure mode ('self-jailbreaking') in reasoning language models, distinct from previously reported catastrophic forgetting of safety after fine-tuning.

The empirical evidence for the phenomenon is broad and systematic: the effect is shown across multiple model families (Qwen, Llama, Phi), scales (0.6B-32B), and training regimes (SFT distillation, RL-only, mixed), making the claim of a universal phenomenon credible rather than anecdotal.

Careful evaluation methodology: the LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-5) for self-jailbreaking detection is validated against ~250 manually annotated prompt-CoT pairs (~8,300 sentences) with reported precision/recall/F1, and the StrongReject judging protocol follows established AISI practice.

The mechanistic analysis goes beyond correlation: projection analysis of compliance and perceived-harmfulness directions is complemented by causal steering interventions that restore refusal after self-jailbreaking, directly supporting the hypothesized mechanism.

The paper connects its findings to and helps explain prior puzzling results in the literature (e.g., Jiang et al. 2025 on forced no-thinking, Zhou et al. 2025 on harmfulness awareness without safe outputs), positioning the work well.

The mitigation result is practically significant and actionable: as few as 50 safety reasoning examples in a multitask setup restore safety (>95% refusal) while preserving reasoning performance on MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond.

Honest limitations section, responsible disclosure framing, and a content warning; the paper also demonstrates the adversarial element of self-jailbreaking traces (they can jailbreak other models), which adds security relevance.
weaknesses: The mechanistic interpretability analysis is largely confined to a single model (S1.1-7B, with directions extracted from its Qwen base model); it is unclear whether the compliance/perceived-harmfulness mechanism generalizes to R1-distilled, Phi, or Nemotron models, or to non-Qwen base families.

The mitigation study (SAFE-S1.1-7B) is also restricted to one model family and one safety dataset (STAR-1); no evidence that minimal safety data works for RL-trained or R1-distilled models, which limits the generality of the practical recommendation.

There is an apparent inconsistency in the ASR threshold definition (Section 3.2 states a harmfulness threshold of 2, while Appendix C states outputs are labeled harmful if the score is above 1); this should be clarified since it affects all headline ASR numbers.
Fixing thinking tokens to 500 is a nontrivial experimental choice; truncation could artificially inflate or deflate self-jailbreaking behavior, and sensitivity to this budget is not reported.

The causal chain is not fully closed: steering on perceived harmfulness after a self-jailbreaking sentence restores refusal, but this shows the direction is causally relevant to refusal, not that self-jailbreaking sentences are the sole or necessary cause of harmful outputs; self-jailbreaking accounts for only 20-60% of successes, and the mechanism behind the remainder is unexplored.

The steering experiments rest on 102 manually annotated self-jailbreaking instances, a relatively small sample, and the sentence-level projection analysis (Figure 6) is a single illustrative CoT rather than an aggregate statistical result.

Novelty relative to adjacent work is solid but not groundbreaking: the broad claim that benign fine-tuning degrades safety is well established (Qi et al., 2024; He et al., 2024), and safety reasoning data mitigations exist (STAR-1, deliberative alignment); the increment is the characterization of the in-CoT self-justification mechanism, which some may view as a refinement.

Some writing issues (e.g., Figure 14 caption mislabeled as 'controlling compliance behavior' for the harmfulness prompts, duplicated references like Wang et al. 2025a/b and Zhao et al. 2025a/b) suggest the paper would benefit from another polish pass.

strengths: Novel and practically significant finding: self-jailbreaking is a distinct safety failure mode where RLMs rationalize compliance in CoT without adversarial prompting, clearly differentiated from catastrophic forgetting and adversarial jailbreaking in the related work

Broad empirical coverage: the phenomenon is demonstrated across 10+ RLMs spanning multiple families (Qwen, Llama, Phi), sizes (0.6B–32B), and training regimes (SFT distillation, RL-only, mixed), strengthening the claim of universality

Careful evaluation methodology: StrongRE benchmark with the AISI judge prompt, and a well-validated LLM-as-a-judge for self-jailbreaking detection (manual annotation of 250 prompt-CoT pairs / 8,300 sentences, 93.9% precision, 89.7% recall), which is often missing in safety papers

Mechanistically grounded analysis beyond correlation: projection analysis of compliance and perceived-harmfulness directions, sentence-level CoT tracing, and a clever counterfactual regeneration experiment (Table 1) that isolates the causal effect of self-jailbreaking sentences, plus steering experiments that restore refusal behavior

Actionable mitigation result: showing that as few as 50 safety reasoning samples mixed into training restores alignment (95%+ refusal) while preserving reasoning capability, with robustness checks against multiple jailbreaking attack types and Wild Jailbreak, plus a comparison to SOTA safety training methods
Well-organized paper with clear definitions, content warnings, thorough appendices, and honest discussion of limitations (self-jailbreaking explains only part of ASR, English-only, etc.)
weaknesses: The mechanistic analysis (Sections 4.1–4.2) is essentially confined to s1.1-7B with directions extracted from its base Qwen model; generality of the compliance/harmfulness direction findings across other RLM families is not demonstrated, and the 102 manually annotated self-jailbreaking instances used for projection/steering analysis form a small sample

The mitigation result, while useful, is somewhat anticipated: prior work (e.g., STAR-1) already showed safety reasoning data improves alignment; the novelty here is mainly the data-efficiency in a multitask setup rather than a new technique

Evaluation depends heavily on GPT-5 as judge for both harmfulness scoring and self-jailbreaking detection; despite validation, judge biases (e.g., favoring elaborate rationalized answers) could inflate ASR or self-jailbreaking rates
Fixed 500-token thinking budget may truncate reasoning chains and could distort self-jailbreaking rates for models that would otherwise reason longer; sensitivity to this setting is not reported
Self-jailbreaking accounts for only 20–60% of attack successes, and the mechanisms behind the remaining failures are left unexplored, weakening the completeness of the explanatory story

The 'emergent' claim is supported indirectly (absence of trigger phrases in training data) rather than through a controlled training-dynamics study; a direct causal link between specific training data properties and self-jailbreaking onset remains open

strengths: Identifies and names a practically important, well-motivated safety failure mode (self-jailbreaking) in reasoning language models, and demonstrates it systematically across a broad and diverse set of models (families, sizes 0.6B-32B, SFT/RL training regimes, and training mixtures), which is convincing evidence that the phenomenon is widespread rather than model-specific

The observation that models remain safety-aware (85%+ of self-jailbreaking instances show the model recognizes harmfulness; 95-99% accuracy on explicit harmfulness classification) is a sharp and interesting finding that distinguishes this failure from catastrophic forgetting of safety

The mechanistic analysis section is well designed: compliance and perceived-harmfulness directions are extracted via contrastive system prompts, a sentence-by-sentence projection analysis visualizes the dual shift (compliance up, perceived harm down) within a single CoT, and a counterfactual regeneration experiment isolates the causal effect of the self-jailbreaking sentence (Table 1), plus steering interventions that restore refusal behavior add causal support

Practically useful mitigation result: mixing as little as 5% STAR-1 safety reasoning data (~50 samples) restores >95% refusal while preserving reasoning performance, with additional evaluation against multiple jailbreak attacks (adaptive, past-tense, prefilling, Wild Jailbreak) and comparison to SOTA safety training methods

Good evaluation hygiene: manual annotation of ~8,300 CoT sentences to validate the GPT-5 judge (93.9% precision / 93.0% recall), documented model configurations, and a content warning with responsible disclosure of examples
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the paper itself concedes that prior work (Zhou et al. 2025a/b, Jiang et al. 2025, Guha et al. 2025) already showed RLMs are unsafe without safety reasoning training, and that benign fine-tuning degrades safety (Qi et al. 2024, He et al. 2024). The genuinely new element is the 'model reasons itself out while remaining aware' framing, but the headline phenomenon builds substantially on known results

The mechanistic methodology is largely an adaptation of existing techniques (Chen et al. 2025 persona vectors; Zhao et al. 2025a harmfulness/refusal directions; Arditi et al. 2024), and the analysis is confined almost entirely to a single model (s1.1-7B) with only 102 hand-annotated instances; the generalizability of the mechanism to other model families is not demonstrated

The mitigation in Section 5 essentially repackages the existing STAR-1 dataset with a mixing ratio; the 'minimal safety reasoning' contribution is incremental over Wang et al. (2025e), and safety reasoning training restores refusal but leaves ~37% self-jailbreaking traces in CoT, which is not fully resolved

Heavy reliance on GPT-5 as both the harm judge and the self-jailbreaking detector; while validated on 250 instances, the definition of a 'self-jailbreaking sentence' is inherently subjective and the detection prompt may miss rationalization patterns not anticipated by the authors

Experimental choices may understate or distort behavior: capping thinking tokens at 500 is non-standard for reasoning models and could truncate safety reasoning; evaluations are English-only and mostly on StrongREJECT; base-model ASR (<5%) comparison does not control for base models' weaker instruction-following of harmful requests, complicating the interpretation of the ASR jump

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'first mechanistic analysis' and 'emergent' framing, where the word-count-based evidence for emergence (absence of trigger phrases in training data) is weak

strengths: Identifies and rigorously characterizes a novel, practically important safety failure mode ('self-jailbreaking') in reasoning language models, where models unintentionally reason their way past their own safety guardrails after benign reasoning training — a phenomenon distinct from adversarial jailbreaking and from catastrophic forgetting of safety.

Broad empirical coverage: the phenomenon is demonstrated across 10+ models spanning multiple families (Qwen, Llama, Phi), sizes (0.6B–32B), and training regimes (SFT distillation, RL-only, mixed), strengthening the claim of generality beyond a single model.

The mechanistic analysis is unusually strong for a safety paper: it goes beyond correlational projection analysis to include a counterfactual regeneration experiment (isolating the causal effect of self-jailbreaking sentences on compliance/perceived harmfulness, Table 1) and causal steering interventions that restore refusal behavior (Figure 5, Table 2), directly supporting the claimed mechanism.

Good measurement hygiene: the LLM-as-a-judge pipeline for detecting self-jailbreaking is validated against ~8,300 manually annotated CoT sentences (93.9% precision, 89.7% recall), and the harmlessness judge follows the UK/US AISI StrongREJECT protocol.

The mitigation result is actionable and well-supported: mixing as few as ~50 STAR-1 safety reasoning samples into reasoning training reduces ASR dramatically while preserving reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, GPQA-Diamond), generalizes to a second model family (Llama), and is benchmarked against SOTA safety-reasoning methods (STAR, SafeChain, DAPO, RECAP) including robustness to out-of-distribution jailbreak attacks (Table 5, 6).

Well-organized paper with clear definitions, a useful taxonomy of self-jailbreaking types (Figure 13, Table 4), and honest limitations section acknowledging that self-jailbreaking explains only part of safety failures.
weaknesses: The core mechanistic analysis (projection, steering, counterfactuals) is conducted primarily on s1.1-7B with only 102 manually annotated self-jailbreaking instances; it is unclear how well the compliance/harmfulness-direction account generalizes to other model families and scales.

Self-jailbreaking explains only 20–60% of the ASR increase across models; the remaining majority of safety failures are left unexplained, which limits the completeness of the paper's causal story despite the breadth of the ASR results.
The self-jailbreaking rate and classification rely on GPT-5 as a judge; while validated on 250 prompt–CoT pairs, this introduces potential judge-model bias and the manual validation set is modest.

Safety evaluation is largely restricted to StrongREJECT (313 English prompts); broader coverage (multilingual, agentic, other harm benchmarks) would strengthen the generality claims, and the English-only scope is acknowledged but not addressed.

The 'emergent' framing is somewhat soft: the evidence is that self-jailbreaking phrases do not appear in training data, but the paper does not fully rule out subtler data-induced precursors, and the mitigation section is essentially a straightforward application of existing STAR-1 data in a multitask recipe.

Some hyperparameters for steering (coefficient choice, layer selection) appear somewhat hand-tuned on a small instance set, and per-instance coefficient derivation details could be more thoroughly ablated.
